title_en: How Sunrise on the Reaping Fits Into the Previous Five Hunger Games Movies... and Whether or Not There Could Be a Seventh Movie
summary_en: The Hunger Games: What you need to know before Sunrise on the Reaping. We break down all the characters, continuity, and Capitol shenanigans.
body_en:
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens in theaters November 20.
As with many other big movie franchises based on pre-existing stories from another medium, The Hunger Games has many fans who’ve immersed themselves in the original book series by Suzanne Collins, but also plenty of others who really only know the world via the films. And for those who’ve only engaged with its dystopian future on-screen since it was introduced in the first Hunger Games movie in 2012, you might be wondering what exactly is going on with this new installment, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.
Where does this sixth installment take place in the history of the series? How does it connect to the last released film, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes? It’s a prequel, right, but also… Jennifer Lawrence appears in it somehow?!
Here’s your overview of the film, based on info from the previous movies and what’s been officially revealed about Sunrise on the Reaping. I won’t be giving any specific spoilers for what occurs in the book upon which it’s based, though its prequel status makes some of the big-picture spoilers more obvious since they’ve been known since the very first movie.
Sunrise on the Reaping is a prequel to the first four Hunger Games films which adapted Collins’ original three books, and takes place 24 years before we were introduced to Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Our main character here is Haymitch Abernanthy, played in the earlier films by Woody Harrelson and now portrayed as a teenager by Joseph Zada (Netflix’s East of Eden). The film depicts the 50th annual Hunger Games, which is also the second “Quarter Quell” edition. This occurs in the games every 25 years; additional twist elements are thrown in by the Capitol beyond the usual awful norm of one boy and one girl being chosen from each of the 12 districts to fight until only one of the 24 kids is left alive. The Quarter Quell concept was first depicted in Catching Fire , which took place at the 75th games and in which previous winners were brought back regardless of their age for a cruel All Stars-type edition.
We already know a few things about the 50th games from the earlier films, starting with the twist that each district had to send four children, not two — two boys and two girls. And we’ve known from the start who won those games: Haymitch, which is why he was the one and only mentor to Katniss and Peeta (Josh Hutcherson), since District 12 had no other winners who could take on that role.
This of course takes away the tension of who will survive the games in Sunrise on the Reaping, given there can only be one winner of the Hunger Games, which is why Katniss’ brave and risky move that got her and Peeta both out alive was such a big deal in the first movie. But that inherent issue is your classic prequel dilemma to solve: How do you create drama when we know the basics of the story’s outcome?
The solution that first Collins and now the filmmakers — including screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie, and director Francis Lawrence (who’s made every Hunger Games movie except the first) — have employed is first by expanding upon who Haymitch was before the Games versus who he became after, given we were introduced to him as a bitter, sardonic drunk. And the other important element is to show the early days of the new rebellion against the Capitol that took center stage as the original films progressed, mainly by depicting several key characters in their younger days who will go on to play important roles later.
This includes previous Hunger Games winners that we saw take part in the third Quarter Quell in Catching Fire, such as Beetee (with Kelvin Harrison Jr. taking over for Jeffrey Wright), Mags (Lily Taylor taking over for Lynn Cohen), and Wiress (Maya Hawke taking over for Amanda Plummer), all of whom we know have no love for the Capitol. There are also prominent characters like Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning taking over for Elizabeth Banks) and Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin taking over for Stanley Tucci) showing up in their earlier days as cogs in the Capitol’s machine, though Effie is destined to have her eyes opened to the darkness of the system she’s a part of in a way Caesar will not.
And then there’s Plutarch Heavensbee, an important figure in the Capitol who was named the head Gamemaker in Catching Fire only to turn out to be actually working against the Capitol from within, secretly helping the rebellion in crucial ways. Jesse Plemons takes on the role played by the late, great Philip Seymour Hoffman in a film that amusingly has two actors playing younger versions of men for whom they once portrayed the onscreen son — Plemons played Hoffman’s son in 2012’s The Master and Harrison Jr. played Wright’s son in 2018’s Monster.
As for the other young Tributes fighting in the Hunger Games alongside Haymitch, they include his fellow District 12 residents Maysilee (McKenna Grace), Wyatt (Ben Wang), and Louella (Molly McCann) among the 48 kids. But again, this is the Hunger Games, and Haymitch is the previously established winner, so… Well, let’s just say that if you like these guys, just be ready to be a bit (or a lot) sad about where things are going.
It was also reported a year ago by the trades and then ultimately confirmed by the actors involved that Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson make appearances in this movie despite the era in which it takes place. Suffice to say, Collins’ book provided a simple way this can occur.
The most recent Hunger Games movie, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , was also a prequel but one set far earlier, during and after the events of the 10th Hunger Games that took place 64 years before Katniss’ first games.
So is there anything that happened in that movie that you should know or be reminded of for Sunrise on the Reaping? Likely not too much, given that the story was centered on the origins of the franchise’s overarching villain, Coriolanus Snow (played in the original films by the late Donald Sutherland), long before most of the other notable characters were even born. The ever-menacing Snow is also in Sunrise on the Reaping, played in his middle-aged era by Ralph Fiennes, though his screen time appears more on par with Sutherland’s as an ominous figure who pops in now and again.
Still, it’s worth brushing up on what that previous film taught us about Snow’s history in regards to District 12. That included how Snow, as a disgraced teenage boy from the Capitol (played in Songbirds & Snakes by Tom Blyth) ended up in a romantic relationship with Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who he had mentored in the 10th Hunger Games, where she ultimately became District 12’s first-ever winner. Even though he and Lucy Gray — who was part of District 12’s nomadic, musically-inclined group called the Covey — entertained the idea of running away together, Snow was unable to suppress his own dark inclinations and quest for power, committing heinous acts including betraying his friend to successfully get back into the Capitol's good graces. Lucy Gray’s discovery of Snow’s actions ultimately led Snow to lash out and try to kill her, shooting at her as she fled into the woods outside District 12.
Lucy Gray’s final fate is unknown, as a body is never found; it’s not clear if she died from injuries trying to escape or survived. If she survived, we don’t know if she ever returned to District 12. However, Snow’s anger at what occurred led him to suppress records of her Hunger Games; he’s unable to erase her existence but does what he can to prevent future generations knowing how District 12 came to have their first and only winner until Haymitch. And all of this also explains why he has a special scorn for District 12 and those who come from that area.
Meanwhile, Suzanne Collins has continued to be vague about Lucy Gray’s fate, even as there are many fan theories regarding her potential survival and the possibility that she had children who lived within District 12. But we know her legacy lives on in some form, as songs she wrote and performed continue to survive decades later, including “The Hanging Tree,” which Katniss sings in Mockingjay – Part 1 .
So now that we’ve gotten two prequel movies, what might be the next installment of the Hunger Games series, presuming Lionsgate wants to make more (and it’s easy to guess they will)?
That answer is unclear. So far, the movies have been strictly based on Collins’ novels, and she hasn’t released any other books since Sunrise. But the announcement that Sunrise was happening as a book was made simultaneously with the announcement of its film adaptation, showing the synergy that has risen between the two. Meanwhile, the franchise’s longtime producer and director, Nina Jacobson and Francis Lawrence, have stated they’d only want to keep making films if Collins gave them new books.
So if she were to return to Panem again, would Collins tell another prequel story or finally delve into an actual sequel? The latter raises tricky questions of whether it would diminish the ending of her book trilogy (and the four films into which it was adapted), presumably requiring some sort of big conflict to break out again à la the Star Wars sequel trilogy.
If it’s another prequel, it might be tricky now to find a story worth telling. Snow’s origins were a compelling topic, and Haymitch’s games were probably the most requested specific storyline for a prequel by fans for many years. Some always suggest going back to the very first Hunger Games, but it feels like that might not offer a lot to make it stand out, given The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes showed us what those early, more bare-bones Hunger Games were like already. Plus, that film covered much of how the Games came to be by introducing us to Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), who came up with the idea of the Hunger Games as a drunken lark only to be horrified when Snow’s father turned them into a reality.
Perhaps, though, something could be done with the first Quarter Quell, AKA the 25th Hunger Games? Now that we’ve seen the second and third “special edition” games, it does feel like we should probably fill in the gap with the first one. Also, intriguingly, almost nothing is known about that Hunger Games — including who won it! — except that the “twist” was that each district was given the awful task of voting on which of their two local children would compete and almost certainly die.
And hey, that sounds like some bleak, dystopian drama ripe for cinematic treatment!
